findings.title: Redaction should be a compiled port of the gitleaks rule set with a measured catch rate, not hand-rolled regexes
findings.problem: "Scrubs common secret patterns" with a "mention its catch rate" is not a spec, and hand-rolled patterns miss the long tail that matters (Slack tokens, Stripe live keys, GCP service-account JSON, JWTs, PEM blocks, postgres:// URLs with inline passwords, high-entropy hex). Meanwhile the hot path budget rules out shelling out to a scanner binary per hook. The good middle path is to take an existing, maintained rule corpus and compile it, but the plan does not name one, does not say where redaction runs relative to the store write, and does not define how catch rate is measured, so the number will be unfalsifiable.
findings.evidence: gitleaks.toml (default config, 222 `[[rules]]` entries, e.g. `id = "anthropic-api-key"` at line 150, `id = "aws-access-token"` at line 206) and `entropy = 3.8` at gitleaks.toml:75, which shows the corpus already pairs each regex with an entropy floor and a global allowlist; VERIFIED_FACTS.md:37 "the plan's '<150 ms hook startup before the network call' is impossible if the hook process imports SQLAlchemy; it is easy (about 25-30 ms) with a stdlib-only hot path."
findings.recommendation: Add to Section 5 a build step `make gen-redact` that reads a vendored, version-pinned `vendor/gitleaks.toml` and emits `src/verdict/core/_redact_rules.py`: one precompiled `re` alternation of the rule regexes plus a per-rule `(id, entropy_floor)` table, plus a Shannon-entropy check (threshold 4.0 over base64/hex runs ≥ 20 chars) for unmatched high-entropy strings. Pure stdlib `re`, no runtime dependency on gitleaks. State in 11 that redaction runs in core, before both the provider client and the store write, so `events.tool_response_json` on disk is already redacted (keep an opt-in `store_raw: false` default). For 8.2, define catch rate concretely: seed 200 synthetic secrets of 20 distinct types into fixture tool outputs, report recall per type and the false-positive rate on a clean 5,000-line corpus, and fail CI if recall on the seeded set drops below 0.95. Also apply the same module server-side in the playground (see SEC-8).

verifier.note: The gitleaks citations are almost all exact against the local copy: `grep -c '^\[\[rules\]\]' gitleaks.toml` = 222, `id = "anthropic-api-key"` is on line 150, `id = "aws-access-token"` on line 206, `entropy = 3.8` on line 75, and the global `[allowlist]` block starts at line 22 -- and the file header confirms it is "the default gitleaks configuration file" (minVersion v8.25.0). VERIFIED_FACTS.md:37 is quoted correctly. One factual overstatement: "the corpus already pairs each regex with an entropy floor" is false -- only 130 of the 222 rules carry an `entropy =` key (58.6%, recomputed with python3: 130/222 = 0.5856). The rest are pure-regex rules with no floor, so the generator must treat the entropy floor as optional per rule rather than assuming one exists. Everything else holds: the plan really does stop at "scrubs common secret patterns ... mention its catch rate" (VERDICT_PLAN.md:322), never says where redaction sits relative to the store write, and a stdlib-only precompiled alternation is the right fit for a ~25-30 ms hot path.
verifier.corrected_recommendation: Same recommendation, with the entropy claim corrected: 130 of gitleaks' 222 default rules carry an `entropy` floor (58.6%), not all of them, so `make gen-redact` must emit `(id, entropy_floor_or_None)` and apply the floor only where the rule defines one, falling back to the global Shannon check (threshold 4.0 over base64/hex runs >= 20 chars) elsewhere. Also port the file's global `[allowlist]` (gitleaks.toml:22 ff.) paths and stopwords, not just the rule regexes, or the false-positive rate on the clean 5,000-line corpus will be dominated by the cases gitleaks already excludes. Add a CI check that `vendor/gitleaks.toml`'s pinned version matches the generated module's recorded `minVersion`.

findings.title: API key: keep it out of shell history, out of hook.log, and out of SDK request-body logging
findings.problem: The plan never says how the Jev key is obtained or protected. The plugin mechanism does the right thing if used correctly — a `sensitive: true` userConfig value goes to the macOS Keychain and is exported to hook processes as an env var — but three leak paths are unaddressed. First, the install CLI accepts the value as a flag, which puts it in shell history and in any CI log. Second, the plan adds `~/.verdict/hook.log` for fail-open exception logging (Phase 2), and an unhandled httpx/requests exception repr commonly carries the request headers. Third, the TypeSafe SDK's own logging redacts secret headers but explicitly does not redact bodies, so a user who sets a debug log level gets their source code written to disk by a library Verdict pulled in.
findings.evidence: cc_plugins_ref.md:618 "All values are exported to hook processes as `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_<KEY>` environment variables, where `<KEY>` is the option key uppercased."; cc_plugins_ref.md:632 "On macOS, Claude Code stores sensitive values in the macOS Keychain, falling back to `~/.claude/.credentials.json`"; typesafe_llms_full.txt:17923 "Secret headers are redacted from log output; request and response bodies are not."; cc_plugins_ref.md:1037 "`--config <key=value>` Set a userConfig option declared in the plugin's manifest."
findings.recommendation: In plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json declare `"userConfig": {"api_key": {"type": "string", "sensitive": true}}` and read it in the hook only as `os.environ["CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_API_KEY"]` — never via `${user_config.API_KEY}` in a shell-form command, which would place it on a command line visible to `ps`. Document in README that the key must be entered at the `/plugin install` prompt, never via `claude plugin install --config api_key=...`. In src/verdict/hooks/cli.py wrap the top-level except in a scrubber that replaces any substring equal to the key value, and any `sk-`/`Bearer ` prefixed token, with `<redacted>` before writing to ~/.verdict/hook.log; add a test that raises an httpx error carrying an Authorization header and asserts the key is absent from the log file. Explicitly set the SDK logger level to WARNING and refuse to start if `TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL` is `debug`, printing "debug logging would write your tool output to disk". Add an assertion in the telemetry client and in every store write path that the key value never appears in the payload.

verifier.note: Three of the four citations are verbatim and correct: cc_plugins_ref.md:618 ("All values are exported to hook processes as `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_<KEY>` environment variables, where `<KEY>` is the option key uppercased"), :632 (macOS Keychain, falling back to ~/.claude/.credentials.json, ~2 KB limit), :1037 (`--config <key=value>`), and typesafe_llms_full.txt:17923 verbatim ("Secret headers are redacted from log output; request and response bodies are not.", repeated at :18183). The three leak paths are real and the plan is silent on all of them. But the stated rationale for avoiding `${user_config.API_KEY}` is inverted. cc_hooks.md:501: "A shell-form plugin hook whose `command` references `${user_config.*}` fails with an error instead of running" -- so the shell-form case the reviewer warns about is already impossible, and cc_plugins_ref.md:620 explains why ("Fields that run in a shell reject `${user_config.*}`"). cc_hooks.md:499 says substitution works "in exec form only: the value is substituted into `command` and into each `args` element as a plain string" -- which is precisely the form that would place the key in argv where `ps` can read it. The advice (read `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_API_KEY` from the environment) is right; only the reason is backwards.
verifier.corrected_recommendation: Same recommendation, with the rationale corrected: do not use `${user_config.API_KEY}` in the hook's *exec-form* `command`/`args`, because that is the only form where substitution happens (cc_hooks.md:499) and it injects the key into the process's argv, visible to `ps` for any local user. Shell form is not the risk -- Claude Code rejects a shell-form plugin hook that references `${user_config.*}` outright (cc_hooks.md:501, cc_plugins_ref.md:620). In both forms, read the key only from `os.environ["CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_API_KEY"]`. Keep the rest as written; also note the ~2 KB Keychain budget shared with OAuth tokens (cc_plugins_ref.md:632) so the manifest does not declare large sensitive values alongside the key.

findings.title: The hosted playground is an unauthenticated Jev proxy on the author's key that collects other people's transcripts
findings.problem: "Paste a Claude Code transcript" means strangers pasting their real sessions — with secrets, internal hostnames, and client code — into a server the author runs, and the only stated controls are "Rate-limit, never store content". Three distinct problems. Abuse: `/v1/playground/verify` is a free Jev endpoint funded by the author's card; a scraper can drive an unbounded bill, and rate-limiting by IP alone is defeated by any proxy pool. Liability: the author becomes the custodian of other people's secrets even transiently, and "no persistence" is false by default because uvicorn/nginx access logs, error tracebacks, and any APM will capture bodies or query strings. Size: a 200 MB pasted transcript is a trivial memory DoS and will blow the 32,000-token context anyway.
findings.evidence: VERDICT_PLAN.md:302 "**Playground:** paste a Claude Code transcript (or pick a sample) → see the compressed ledger, each question's probability, and the action Verdict would take. Rate-limit, never store content."; VERIFIED_FACTS.md:32 "context 32,000 tokens; price $0.042 per 1M input tokens"
findings.recommendation: Write into 9.2: request body cap of 1 MB enforced at the reverse proxy and again in FastAPI (`Content-Length` check before reading), reject above; run the SEC-6 redaction module server-side on the pasted text before the provider call and show the user the redacted ledger so the redaction is visible; per-IP token bucket of 5/hour plus a global daily spend ceiling read from the `usage.cost` field OpenRouter returns, with the endpoint returning 503 and a static sample result once 80% of the ceiling is hit; disable body logging explicitly (uvicorn `--access-log` off or a log filter dropping the body and query string, no Sentry `send_default_pii`); and set a `no-store` policy documented on the page. Add a second mode, shipped first if time is short: a pure-browser playground where the user supplies their own key and the request goes direct from the page to the provider — but verify the provider sends permissive CORS headers before promising this, which is unverified today.

verifier.note: VERDICT_PLAN.md:302 quoted verbatim, and VERIFIED_FACTS.md:32 confirms the 32,000-token context and $0.042/1M input pricing, and that OpenRouter's response "adds id, provider, usage.cost" -- so the proposed spend ceiling has a real field to read. The abuse, custodianship and size arguments all hold, and nothing in the plan caps request size, meters spend, or specifies auth for the endpoint. One correction: "the only stated controls are 'Rate-limit, never store content'" is not accurate -- VERDICT_PLAN.md:323 adds "Hosted playground: rate-limited, no persistence of submitted content, no logging of bodies." That is still only a statement of intent with no mechanism, which is the finding's real point, but the finding should not claim the plan is silent on body logging. The browser-direct fallback is correctly labeled unverified; I did not re-test CORS on api.typesafe.ai or openrouter.ai, and VERIFIED_FACTS.md records nothing about CORS headers either way.
verifier.corrected_recommendation: Same recommendation, with the framing corrected: VERDICT_PLAN.md:323 already promises "no logging of bodies" for the hosted playground, so the gap is that no mechanism enforces it -- specify the mechanism (uvicorn `--access-log` off or a log filter dropping body and query string, no Sentry `send_default_pii`, no APM body capture) rather than introducing the requirement as new. Everything else stands: 1 MB body cap at the proxy and again in FastAPI via `Content-Length` before reading, the SEC-6 redactor run server-side with the redacted ledger shown back to the user, a per-IP token bucket plus a global daily ceiling accumulated from OpenRouter's `usage.cost` (VERIFIED_FACTS.md:32) returning 503 plus a static sample at 80%, and a documented no-store policy. Keep the browser-direct mode explicitly conditional on a CORS preflight check against the chosen provider host, which is still unverified.

findings.title: Local dashboard: stored XSS from tool output, plus no binding, token, CSRF or Host check on the label endpoints
findings.problem: The dashboard renders `events.tool_response_json`, which contains bytes the agent fetched from the internet or read out of a repo. A session timeline that interpolates that into HTML gives any web page the agent visited stored XSS in a localhost origin that also has a write endpoint (label mode) and read access to every raw tool input in the database. Separately, the plan says only "starts on localhost": no explicit bind address (FastAPI/uvicorn's habit of `0.0.0.0` in examples would expose the DB to the coffee-shop LAN), no auth token, no CSRF protection on the label POST, and no Host header check, so any site the user visits can POST to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/labels` (writes) and, via DNS rebinding, read the JSON endpoints too.
findings.evidence: VERDICT_PLAN.md:101 "`verdict-dashboard` | FastAPI + HTMX or a small React/Vite app | Local: `verdict dashboard` starts on localhost. Reads store, renders sessions, verdicts, calibration plots." and VERDICT_PLAN.md:221 "label mode (click to label an event → writes `labels`)"
findings.recommendation:
Specify in 9: bind `127.0.0.1` explicitly (`uvicorn.run(host="127.0.0.1", port=0)`), take an ephemeral port, and mint a 32-byte `secrets.token_urlsafe()` per launch that must appear as `?t=` on first load and is then set as a `HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookie; reject any request whose `Host` header is not `127.0.0.1:` or `localhost:` (blocks DNS rebinding); send no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header at all; require the token in an `X-Verdict-Token` header on every POST to `/labels` and `/outcomes`. Escape all stored content — with Jinja2 set `autoescape=True` and never use `|safe` on an events column; render tool output inside `
` with a `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; style-src 'self'; script-src 'self'` response header. Add tests/integration/test_dashboard_security.py with four cases: a `` payload in a stored tool_response renders escaped; a POST without the token returns 403; a request with `Host: evil.com` returns 421; the listening socket is not reachable from a non-loopback address.

verifier.note: Both plan quotes verbatim: VERDICT_PLAN.md:101 ("Local: `verdict dashboard` starts on localhost. Reads store, renders sessions, verdicts, calibration plots.") and :221 ("label mode (click to label an event -> writes `labels`)"). I grepped the whole plan for `127.0.0.1`, `0.0.0.0`, `CSRF`, `token`, `autoescape` -- the only hits for `localhost` are lines 101 and 221 and there are no hits for any of the others, so the plan genuinely specifies no bind address, no auth, no CSRF defense and no Host check. The stored-XSS source is real: `events.tool_response_json` is the raw tool response (VERDICT_PLAN.md:108) and the timeline renders each event (VERDICT_PLAN.md:221). Every control proposed is standard and implementable: `uvicorn.run(host="127.0.0.1", port=0)` binds an ephemeral loopback port, Jinja2 `autoescape=True` is the documented default for `.html` templates, the Host-header allowlist is the accepted DNS-rebinding defense, and 421 Misdirected Request is a reasonable status for it. The four proposed tests are all mechanically checkable.

findings.title: Gold-set collection from friends' sessions needs a written consent and scrubbing process, and only derived features should ever be committed
findings.problem: Section 8.1 plans to build the reporting set from "3-5 friends/classmates with Verdict installed", and Section 5 puts `data/goldset/` in the public repo. Those sessions contain their employers' code, internal hostnames and, given SEC-6 has no measured recall yet, live credentials. "With consent" is doing all the work and is not a process: there is no consent artifact, no scrubbing step, no second-person review before commit, and no revocation path once the data is in git history where a rewrite is the only remedy. Section 7's non-negotiable ("no test ever needs a real transcript from someone else committed to the repo") already states the right rule but Section 8.1 quietly contradicts it for the gold set.
findings.evidence: VERDICT_PLAN.md:262 "**Sources:** (a) your own sessions across 4+ repos; (b) 3–5 friends/classmates with Verdict installed and label mode on (consent + they label their own)" vs VERDICT_PLAN.md:254 "Non-negotiables: hooks fail open; no test ever needs a real transcript from someone else committed to the repo (use the synthetic generator + your own)."
findings.recommendation: Extend the Section 7 non-negotiable to cover data/goldset and state it in 8.1: contributed real events are never committed. Commit only a derived feature row with a fixed, content-free schema — `{contributor_id, event_id_hash, hook_kind, tool_name, status, exit_code, output_len, n_error_rows, n_claim_verbs, claim_verb_set, jev_probabilities{}, label, labeler, ts_day}` — plus fully synthetic events for anything requiring text. Add `docs/CONSENT.md` with a one-page form the contributor signs naming what leaves their machine, that a third-party API sees it, and how to revoke; require a signed copy on file before enabling their `verdict export --goldset`. Make that command refuse without `--i-have-written-consent <contributor_id>`, run the SEC-6 redactor, drop every free-text column, print a diff of the exact rows for human review, and write `data/goldset/PROVENANCE.md` recording contributor_id, date, consent reference and row count. Implement `verdict goldset revoke <contributor_id>` that deletes those rows and add a check in `make eval` that every row's contributor_id appears in PROVENANCE.md.

verifier.note: The contradiction is real and both sides are quoted verbatim. VERDICT_PLAN.md:262: "**Sources:** (a) your own sessions across 4+ repos; (b) 3-5 friends/classmates with Verdict installed and label mode on (consent + they label their own); (c) synthetic perturbations (auto-labeled)." VERDICT_PLAN.md:254: "Non-negotiables: hooks fail open; no test ever needs a real transcript from someone else committed to the repo (use the synthetic generator + your own)." Section 5's repo layout does place `data/goldset/` in the public repo (VERDICT_PLAN.md, Section 5 tree). The residual-risk argument chains correctly off SEC-6 (no measured redaction recall yet) and off the ~300 manually labeled real events target at VERDICT_PLAN.md:263. The proposed derived-feature schema is content-free and still supports every metric in 8.2 (per-question precision/recall/calibration need only the probability, the label and the question key). Consent artifact, provenance file, `--i-have-written-consent` gate, revoke command and the `make eval` PROVENANCE cross-check are all feasible and proportionate.

findings.title: Local store holds raw tool inputs and outputs in plaintext with no permissions, retention window, or purge command
findings.problem: `events` is specified as raw tool_input_json and tool_response_json in `~/.verdict/verdict.db`, and the plan's only privacy statement about it is "never uploaded". Nothing sets file permissions, so the DB inherits the umask and is world-readable on a default macOS umask of 022; nothing bounds retention, so after months of dogfooding the file is a single grep away from every secret the agent ever printed; and there is no purge. This is also the file a user would attach to a bug report. The hooks reference's own security guidance for hook authors is to avoid touching this class of data at all, which makes storing it by default a deliberate choice that needs a deliberate control.
findings.evidence: VERDICT_PLAN.md:108 "`events(id, session_id, seq, kind[pre|post|stop|subagent_stop], tool_name, tool_input_json, tool_response_json, ts)` — raw, local only, never uploaded."; cc_hooks.md:3794 "**Skip sensitive files**: avoid `.env`, `.git/`, keys, etc."
findings.recommendation: In src/verdict/store/db.py create `~/.verdict` with mode 0o700 and chmod the DB plus its `-wal` and `-shm` sidecars to 0o600 on every open (WAL mode creates them fresh). Add `retention_days: 30` to policies/default.yaml and a purge that runs on session start: delete `events` rows older than the window while keeping `verdicts`, `actions` and `labels`, which carry no content. Ship `verdict purge [--all | --session <id> | --older-than <days>]` and `verdict export --support-bundle` that includes only verdicts/actions/latency and never the `events` raw columns. Add a `store_raw: true|false` policy key (default true locally, documented) and, when false, store only the redacted projection. Note the retention window and the DB path verbatim in docs/PRIVACY.md and in the `verdict init` disclosure.

verifier.note: VERDICT_PLAN.md:108 quoted verbatim, including "-- raw, local only, never uploaded." cc_hooks.md:3794 quoted verbatim ("**Skip sensitive files**: avoid `.env`, `.git/`, keys, etc."), inside the hooks reference's "Security best practices" list, so the reviewer's framing of it as guidance to hook authors is accurate. I grepped the plan for `retention`, `purge`, `chmod` and `0600`: zero hits, so there is genuinely no permissions, retention or purge story. The umask claim is correct -- SQLite creates the database file 0666 & ~umask, giving 0644 under the macOS default 022, and WAL mode creates `-wal`/`-shm` sidecars the same way, which is why the recommendation to chmod all three on every open (not just at create) is the right shape. Keeping `verdicts`/`actions`/`labels` past the retention window while purging `events` is coherent with the data model at VERDICT_PLAN.md:109-112, which holds no raw content.

findings.title: Telemetry is pseudonymous, not anonymous, and the "N installs" headline rides on an unauthenticated ingest endpoint
findings.problem: The field list is genuinely content-free, but the plan calls it "anonymous" twice. `install_id_hash` plus a precise `ts` plus `plugin_version` reconstructs one machine's working hours, session shapes and upgrade timeline; the collector and any reverse proxy in front of it log client IPs by default, which re-identifies the id; and `latency_ms` at full precision is a weak network fingerprint. Separately, install count is a headline number in Sections 1 and 12 and is computed from distinct ids arriving at a public unauthenticated endpoint, so anyone who reads the source can mint a million ids and either inflate the number or, more damagingly, make it untrustworthy right when the blog post cites it.
findings.evidence: VERDICT_PLAN.md:113 "`telemetry_events` (hosted only): `install_id_hash, plugin_version, event_kind, question_key, probability_bucket, action, latency_ms, ts`. **No content, no paths, no tool inputs. Ever.**" and VERDICT_PLAN.md:36 "Opt-in anonymous telemetry powering a public live stats page."
findings.recommendation: Change the wording everywhere from "anonymous" to "pseudonymous, content-free" and say why in docs/PRIVACY.md. Derive `install_id_hash` as HMAC-SHA256 of a locally generated random 16-byte salt (never of hostname, username, cwd or MAC) and rotate it on the 1st of each month so cross-month linkage is impossible; store the salt in ~/.verdict/telemetry_id with mode 0600. Coarsen `ts` to the hour and replace `latency_ms` with a bucket enum (`<100, 100-300, 300-600, 600-1000, >1000`). Configure the reverse proxy to log no client IP (`log_format` without `$remote_addr`) and set the FastAPI app to never persist one; state that in the privacy page. Ship `verdict telemetry preview` printing the exact JSON body for the last 10 events, `verdict telemetry off`, and honour `VERDICT_TELEMETRY=off` as an override that wins over config. For stats integrity: apply a per-IP ingest cap at the proxy, require each install to include an HMAC over its id using a key derived from a lightweight one-time registration, and publish installs from PyPI download counts and marketplace numbers alongside the telemetry figure — label the telemetry figure "opted-in installs (self-reported, unverified)" on the stats page.

verifier.note: The substance is right. VERDICT_PLAN.md:113 is verbatim, including "**No content, no paths, no tool inputs. Ever.**", and the plan does call the telemetry "anonymous" twice (line 35 and line 102) plus once more at line 321. The pseudonymity argument is sound and the ingest endpoint is indeed unauthenticated by omission (Section 10 line 313 and the load test at line 251 target `/v1/telemetry` with no auth mentioned). Two corrections. (1) The citation is off by one: "Opt-in anonymous telemetry powering a public live stats page." is VERDICT_PLAN.md:35, not :36; line 36 is "Blog post with real numbers; listed in plugin marketplace(s); >=50 installs in first two weeks", which is the install-count headline the second half of the finding relies on -- so both quotes exist, but they are swapped. (2) Monthly rotation of `install_id_hash` conflicts with the plan's own metrics: VERDICT_PLAN.md:292 lists "Installs (unique hashed ids), weekly active installs ... plugin version distribution", and a rotating id makes cumulative unique installs uncountable and inflates the total by roughly one new id per install per month. verifier.corrected_recommendation: Same recommendation with the citation fixed (telemetry wording at VERDICT_PLAN.md:35 and :102 and :321; install-count headline at :36 and :351-353) and the rotation made metric-aware: keep the locally generated random 16-byte salt in ~/.verdict/telemetry_id at 0600 and HMAC the id from it, but rotate on a cadence the metrics can absorb -- either keep the id stable and drop the cumulative-installs metric in favour of "active installs in the last 30 days", or rotate monthly and relabel VERDICT_PLAN.md:292's "Installs (unique hashed ids)" as "monthly active installs", since cumulative uniques are not recoverable across rotations. findings.title: Supply chain: plugin updates execute on users' machines every session, and the documented bootstrap pattern installs dependencies from the network with no integrity check
findings.problem: A Claude Code plugin is code that runs with the user's full privileges on every tool call and every stop, and updates reach installed users without a review step. The plan's CI section ends at "publish to PyPI + push images" with no word on how the publish is authenticated, and the Actions are unpinned by default, so a compromised third-party action or a stolen PyPI token becomes root-equivalent on every install. If Verdict follows the documented plugin bootstrap pattern to build a Python environment at SessionStart, it will also run an unpinned installer from the network at session start — arbitrary code from a package's build step, on a machine the plugin was trusted to protect.
findings.evidence: cc_hooks.md:3774 "Command hooks execute shell commands with your full user permissions. They can modify, delete, or access any files your user account can access."; cc_plugins_ref.md:776 shows the recommended pattern as `"command": "diff -q \"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/package.json\" \"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/package.json\" >/dev/null 2>&1 || (cd \"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}\" && cp \"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/package.json\" . && npm install)" — an unpinned network install with no hash verification

SCOPE.summary: The plan is a good 12-week plan wearing a 5-week label. Summing the work each phase actually names — mypy --strict core at 90% coverage, SQLAlchemy+Alembic store, a web dashboard with a calibration page, a synthetic perturbation generator, 300 hand labels, LLM-judge baselines, a hosted FastAPI+Postgres+Vercel stack with playground, telemetry, Docker, k6 and Prometheus — lands around 190-275 hours against roughly 75-100 hours available to a part-time student. More damaging than the total is the shape: nothing publishable exists before day 21, and the first real data is scheduled to start on day 6-10 while the friends who supply corpus diversity are recruited on day 29-35. Labeled real data is the one resource that cannot be compressed by working harder, and the plan's own target (≥60 positives per question) is arithmetically out of reach: jev-belay needed 2,694 stops to yield a 100-stop audit slice with 12 positives, and it settled for a model-proxy labeler rather than hand labels. Meanwhile the differentiator the plan never names is sitting in the hooks reference: PostToolUseFailure delivers a top-level `error` string with an `Exit code N` first line, which is exactly the ground truth jev-belay has to reconstruct with two regex belts over ~25 named runners, and it covers the no-edit turns jev-belay publishes as its blind spot. That is a 5-7 day v0.1 that is already differentiated. Three of the plan's headline commitments are unmeasurable or blocked as written: install counts (telemetry is default-off and no marketplace install counter is documented), the brand (PyPI `verdict`, npm `verdict` and the GitHub user `Verdict` are all taken, the PyPI one by an LLM-judge library in the same problem space), and most phase acceptance criteria ("no session ever hangs", "you can label 50 events in <15 minutes"). The fix is a decisive cut of everything hosted, a collector shipped on day 3, and a benchmark that treats jev-belay as a credited baseline arm rather than a threat.

findings.title: The smallest differentiated v0.1 is a PostToolUseFailure-derived failure ledger, and the plan never mentions the event that makes it differentiated
findings.problem: Section 4.2 builds the failure recorder on PostToolUse, which per the verified facts fires only on success; tool failures fire the separate PostToolUseFailure event. That is not just a bug, it is the entire competitive wedge and the plan throws it away. jev-belay reconstructs "did a check run and pass" with two regex belts over a hardcoded list of ~25 runners, precisely because the transcript hides exit codes; its published limits are that a custom check script is invisible unless the user names it in a regex option, and that a turn with no file edits never reaches the question at all. PostToolUseFailure hands you the exit code directly, for any command in any language including `./check.sh`, and it fires on no-edit turns. Building the Stop verifier's ledger from hook events instead of transcript regexes is a real, demonstrable, one-sentence differentiator that costs 5-7 days, and it also produces free weak labels (`Exit code N` is ground truth for `error_present`), which directly relieves the labeling bottleneck in DATA-1.

findings.title: The gold-set target (300 hand labels, ≥60 positives per question) is arithmetically unreachable in 35 days and `dangerous` is unreachable at any scale from real sessions
findings.problem: jev-belay's published corpus is the only measurement of base rates that exists for this problem, and it says: 2,694 real stops produced a 100-stop audit slice of edit-turns containing 12 positives (~12% prevalence), and only 17.7% of all stops even reach the gate. To collect 60 positives on `unreported_failure` at 12% prevalence you need ~500 labeled edit-turn stops, which means roughly 1,000-1,700 raw stops. At an optimistic 30 stops/day of genuine part-time use (unverified rate), that is 33-55 days of uninterrupted collection starting on day 1 — and the plan does not start collecting until day 6-10. Worse, the plan demands the same ≥60 positives for `dangerous` at PreToolUse; the prevalence of a genuinely irreversible destructive command in a student's own sessions is unverified but plainly a small fraction of one percent, so 60 natural positives would require tens of thousands of tool calls. jev-belay also did not hand-label: it used a `claude -p --model sonnet` proxy labeler and published that limitation. Chasing 300 hand labels is both slower and less honest than copying that method and auditing a subset.

EVAL.summary: The evaluation design in Sections 4, 7 and 8 is structurally sensible (frozen reporting split, baselines, calibration as the headline) but the numbers it would produce cannot carry the claims the plan wants to make, and two of its factual premises about Jev are wrong. At the planned n=300 real events with 60 positives per key, the 95% CI half-width is ±7.7–10.0 points on recall, ±10.4 points on AUPRC, and ±10.5 points on a paired Jev-vs-baseline AUPRC difference — wide enough that almost any comparison in the blog post will be unfalsifiable. Worse, ECE with 10 equal-width bins is meaningless at that n: I simulated a *perfectly calibrated* model with a realistic bimodal score distribution and it scores mean ECE 0.040 (p95 0.057) at n=300, with 4 of 10 bins holding fewer than 10 items, and a genuinely miscalibrated model (γ=1.6) overlaps the calibrated null 34.9% of the time. Two Jev premises are wrong against the docs: the acceptance criterion asserts "Jev is stochastic" when TypeSafe says System One "is designed to return stable answers across repeated evaluations" and its own consistency cookbook explicitly disclaims measuring identical-input variance, and Section 8.2 thresholds on a `confidence` field that Noul answers do not have — which is five of the eight shipped questions. The "mean ± std over 3 runs" ritual therefore reports the wrong variance component, roughly 9x smaller than the sampling uncertainty it will be mistaken for. Tuning thresholds on trivially-separable synthetic perturbations and shipping them onto real data invites both distribution shift and outright label leakage (the injected error becomes the ledger's own `status` field). The headline "unsupported-success-claim rate" has no defined denominator and, drawn from the author plus 3–5 friends, has a design effect near 6 that widens a 30% rate to ±12 points. "Recovery rate" and "the nudge changes behavior" are causal claims with no control arm, and the CI guard "precision drops >5 points" fires on pure noise 11–17% of the time at realistic fixture sizes. Everything below is fixable with a bigger reporting set, an item bootstrap, pre-registration, a shadow arm keyed on `prompt_id`, and honest interval reporting.

findings.title: n=300 with 60 positives cannot support any of the published comparisons; CI half-widths are ±8–10 points

Precision is worse than recall here because its denominator is predicted positives, which at a high threshold can be 20-40 items, not 300. The plan never states a denominator target for precision at all.

findings.title: ECE with 10 equal-width bins at n=300 is indistinguishable from noise; a perfectly calibrated model scores 0.040
findings.problem: Calibration is the headline chart and the one number a TypeSafe engineer will scrutinise, and the chosen estimator cannot measure it at this n. I simulated a perfectly calibrated model with a realistic bimodal probability distribution (3000 trials per n): at n=300 the 10-equal-width-bin ECE has mean 0.0398 and p95 0.0567; at n=100 mean 0.0677. So publishing 'ECE = 0.04' at n=300 is publishing the estimator's own bias, not Jev's miscalibration. Bin occupancy is the cause: at n=300 the ten equal-width bins held [91, 38, 17, 5, 1, 3, 9, 15, 22, 99] items — 4 of 10 bins had fewer than 10 items, and the reliability diagram will show wildly noisy midrange points. A discrimination test confirms it: a genuinely overconfident model (γ=1.6 recalibration) produces mean ECE 0.0608 at n=300 and overlaps the calibrated null's p95 34.9% of the time; at n=1000 the overlap is 0.0%.

findings.title: "Jev is stochastic; report mean ± std over 3 runs" contradicts the TypeSafe docs and reports the wrong variance component
findings.problem: Two errors in one sentence. First, the docs do not say Jev is stochastic on identical input — they say the opposite, and the one experiment that looks like it measures this explicitly disclaims doing so: both consistency cookbooks inject a fresh throwaway `uid` into the state on every repeat and note that the setup 'cannot separate sensitivity to the irrelevant field from variation that would occur on identical requests' (typesafe_llms_full.txt:6165). A TypeSafe engineer will read 'Jev is stochastic' in your report and stop reading. Second, even taking the cookbook's measured variance at face value (mean per-question noul std 0.0102 over 15 repeats, typesafe_llms_full.txt:5993), std over 3 runs is the wrong uncertainty to publish: the 95% half-width of a 3-run mean probability is 1.2 probability points, while the sampling half-width on recall at 60 positives is 7.7–10.0 points — a factor of ~9. I also simulated what run-to-run noise can actually do to a metric: with sd=0.0102 on 300 items, a rerun moves a median of 1.2 items (p95 = 3) across a 0.75 threshold, capping the metric shift at ~5.0 recall points even in the worst case where every flip is a positive. Reporting '±0.01' next to a number whose real interval is ±0.10 is the single most attackable thing in the plan.

findings.title: Tuning on synthetic and reporting on real is not enough: no real tuning split, no pre-registration, no defined hash
findings.problem: 'Never tune on the reporting set' is the right instinct but the protocol as written has three holes. (1) There is no *real* tuning split. Thresholds chosen on synthetic perturbations are being transported to a different distribution and a different label definition — the synthetic label is 'I injected an error', the human label is 'a reasonable reviewer would call this an unacknowledged failure'. Those are not the same event, so the transported threshold is not merely noisy, it is aimed at the wrong target. (2) 'Freeze the reporting set with a hash' names no hash, no file, and no enforcement, so nothing stops a later run from silently adding events. (3) Nothing is pre-registered. With ~8 question keys × 3 metrics × several thresholds, the garden of forking paths is wide enough that some question will look great by chance — and at the intervals in EVAL-1, chance is the dominant effect.
findings.evidence: /Users/ronitkatikaneni/Downloads/VERDICT_PLAN.md:229 — "Tune default policy thresholds on the **synthetic** set; report on the **manual** set. Never tune on the reporting set." and :265 — "**Splits:** synthetic → tuning; manual → reporting. Freeze the reporting set with a hash before you tune anything."
findings.recommendation: Replace 8.1's Splits bullet with a three-way split, split *by session* not by event (events within a session are correlated): (a) `synthetic/` — question wording and prompt iteration only, never threshold selection; (b) `real-tune/` — 40% of labeled real sessions, where thresholds are selected; (c) `real-report/` — the remaining 60%, frozen. Freeze mechanically: `make freeze-reporting-set` writes `data/goldset/REPORTING_SET.sha256` containing sha256 of the sorted JSONL of `(event_id, question_key, label)` triples, and `make eval` aborts with a non-zero exit if the recomputed digest differs. Add `docs/EVAL_PREREG.md`, committed and git-tagged `prereg-v1` *before* the first read of `real-report/`, containing: the exact metric list, the primary endpoint (one metric on one question key), the threshold-selection rule stated as an algorithm, the target n, and the analysis code path. Any metric not in that file is reported in the paper under a heading 'exploratory, not pre-registered'.

findings.title: The synthetic generator leaks its own labels into the state and produces trivially separable positives
findings.problem: 'Flip a tool result to an error but keep the success claim' produces a positive that the compressor itself marks: 4.3 builds each ledger row with `status[ok|error|unknown]` derived 'from PostToolUse verdicts when available, else heuristics', so the injected error becomes a literal `status: error` token sitting next to an unqualified success claim. Detecting that is string matching, not judgment, and Jev — which the docs describe as reading questions literally and being 'quite literal in its understanding' — will score near 1.0. Every metric tuned on that set is tuned on an easy distribution, which is precisely how a threshold arrives at real data too permissive or too strict. Second problem: the synthetic set has no realism check at all. Real failures, per the verified facts, arrive through a *separate* `PostToolUseFailure` event whose `error` string starts with `Exit code N` for Bash and is middle-truncated by Claude Code — nothing in the generator reproduces that shape. Third: the 500 synthetic events are auto-labeled and will inevitably appear in a blog post next to the 300 hand-labeled ones, where a reader cannot tell which number is which.

CC.summary: From the Claude Code integration lens (facts the orchestrator has not yet personally verified), the plan is directionally sound on the hooks it names but is missing the single most important comparison point: Claude Code ships native `type:"prompt"` and `type:"agent"` Stop hooks (and the `/goal` command, which is literally documented as a wrapper around a prompt-based Stop hook) that are functionally the same 'LLM judge Stop hook' the plan treats as a slow, expensive alternative in Section 1 and as a novel post-v1 extension in Section 15.3 -- this needs to become a baseline in Section 8.3, not a footnote. Two concrete mechanics in the plan are simply wrong as documented: the Section 4.3 'flag' path relies on stderr, which Claude Code never surfaces to the user on an allow-stop (only JSON `systemMessage` does), and the Section 2.2 'Stop ≤ 1.5s' figure is actually the SessionEnd hook's hard budget, not Stop's (Stop defaults to 600s). Several Phase 2/7 engineering details are underspecified in ways that matter: matcher syntax has no built-in tool-exclusion keyword (a hand-written negative-lookahead regex is required), shell-form Python hook commands can fail silently and differently per OS, headless `--include-hook-events` with `--output-format stream-json` gives a much better E2E assertion mechanism than the plan currently describes, and `claude plugin eval` offers a ready-made WITH/WITHOUT-plugin CI harness with real but limited (code-free) graders. None of these are fatal to the architecture, but each is a specific, sourced correction the plan should incorporate before Phase 2 hook-config work begins.

findings.title: Shell-form Python hook commands can fail silently and cross-platform, disabling the safety gate with no visible error
findings.problem: The plan's hook CLI is invoked as a bare command (implied `verdict hook pre|post|stop`) with no stated exec-form/args split. Shell-form hook commands run through a different shell per OS (sh on macOS/Linux, Git Bash or PowerShell on Windows), and any hook that fails to start (wrong interpreter name, no venv on PATH) becomes a non-blocking error that is never surfaced to the user -- exactly the failure mode that would defeat Verdict's own safety gate.
findings.evidence: 'Shell form ... The `command` string is passed to a shell: `sh -c` on macOS and Linux, Git Bash on Windows, or PowerShell when Git Bash isn't installed.' -- cc_hooks.md:472. '... a mistyped path in `settings.json` leaves the gate silently disabled.' -- cc_hooks.md:860-861 (paraphrase boundary at 'Failed with non-blocking status code' notice, same paragraph).
findings.recommendation: Ship the plugin's `hooks.json` in exec form (`"command": "<absolute-python-path>", "args": [...]`) with the interpreter path resolved and written at install time by `verdict init` (e.g., via `sys.executable`), not a bare shell-form `python3` invocation. Add a Phase 2 acceptance test: on a machine with no `python3` on PATH, confirm the failure is visible (e.g., via `--debug`) rather than silently disabling the gate.

verifier.note: The exec/shell-form quote is verbatim at cc_hooks.md:472, and the "a mistyped path in `settings.json` leaves the gate silently disabled" clause is verbatim at cc_hooks.md:861. But the problem statement overstates invisibility: the same sentence at 861 says a hook that can't start produces the standard notice ("the transcript shows a `<hook name> hook error` notice followed by the first line of stderr, prefixed with `Failed with non-blocking status code:`", cc_hooks.md:859-861; exit 127 for a missing interpreter), matching VERIFIED_FACTS.md A.9. So the failure IS surfaced in the transcript — the real hazard is that it does not block, and that users ignore the notice. The recommendation's mechanism is also wrong: `verdict init` cannot write an install-time interpreter path into the plugin's own `hooks.json`, because marketplace-installed plugins are copied to a cache that is replaced on update (VERIFIED_FACTS.md B.4) and the plan's `verdict init` (VERDICT_PLAN.md:215) merges hook config into settings.json, a different file.
verifier.corrected_recommendation: Ship `plugin/hooks/hooks.json` in exec form (set `args`, cc_hooks.md:470-472) with the interpreter resolved from a path placeholder rather than an install-time rewrite of the plugin's own files: either `"command": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/verdict-hook"` with a bundled launcher, or `"command": "${user_config.PYTHON}"` (placeholder substitution works only in exec form, VERIFIED_FACTS.md B.2), with the venv itself created under CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA by a SessionStart hook (the documented pattern, VERIFIED_FACTS.md B.3). Reserve `sys.executable`-baked absolute paths for the settings.json path that `verdict init` writes, not for the plugin package. Keep the Phase 2 acceptance test, but phrase the assertion correctly: on a machine with no python3 on PATH, assert the transcript shows the `Failed with non-blocking status code:` hook-error notice AND that Verdict fails open (the tool call / stop proceeds), rather than claiming the failure is invisible.

findings.title: No built-in matcher syntax excludes read-only tools; Section 4.1/4.5's 'skip Jev for read-only tools' requires an explicit hand-written regex
findings.problem: The plan assumes PreToolUse can cheaply 'skip Jev for read-only tools by policy' (Section 14) but never states how. Claude Code's matcher is either an exact-string set or, the moment any other character appears, an unanchored JavaScript regex tested with `RegExp.prototype.test` -- there is no dedicated 'exclude' keyword.
findings.evidence: 'Only letters, digits, `_`, `-`, spaces, `,`, and `\|`' → exact match; 'Contains any other character' → 'JavaScript regular expression, unanchored' -- cc_hooks.md:290-293. `mcp__memory__.*` and `mcp__.*__write.*` are given as the only documented wildcard forms (cc_hooks.md:369-371); no negative-match example appears anywhere in the matcher section.
findings.recommendation: Write the exclusion explicitly, e.g. a PreToolUse hook entry with `"matcher": "^(?!Read$|Glob$|Grep$|WebSearch$).*$"`, and put this literal string in `plugin/hooks/hooks.json` and Section 4.1, plus a unit test asserting the hook process is never invoked for a bare `Read` call (verify via absence of a store row, not just a passive verdict).

verifier.note: Matcher evidence is accurate: cc_hooks.md:292-293 gives the exact-string vs unanchored-JS-regex split, :295 confirms `RegExp.prototype.test`, and :369-375 gives `mcp__memory__.*` / `mcp__.*__write.*` as the only wildcard forms. I searched the whole matcher section and found no negative-match example and no `exclude` keyword, and the only other filter, the `if` field (cc_hooks.md:426), holds exactly one permission rule with no negation or combination syntax — so the core claim stands. The proposed `^(?!Read$|Glob$|Grep$|WebSearch$).*$` is valid and works under `RegExp.prototype.test`. Two corrections: (a) the plan is not actually broken — VERDICT_PLAN.md:373 says "skip Jev for read-only tools by policy", i.e. inside the hook, which is workable (~25-30 ms stdlib-only startup, VERIFIED_FACTS.md D) and only wastes process spawns; the matcher is an optimization, so "medium" overstates it; (b) the recommendation must scope the exclusion to the PreToolUse handler only.
verifier.corrected_recommendation: Add an explicit PreToolUse matcher `"^(?!Read$|Glob$|Grep$|WebSearch$).*$"` in `plugin/hooks/hooks.json` and document it in Section 4.1 as an optimization over the in-hook policy skip (which remains the correctness-bearing path, since a matcher cannot express per-argument conditions). Apply it ONLY to the PreToolUse handler — leaving PostToolUse/PostToolUseFailure unmatchered, or the Stop verifier's tool ledger loses read-tool rows. Test by asserting no PreToolUse row is written for a bare `Read`, while the PostToolUse row for that same call still exists.

findings.title: Undefined plugin version strategy risks either update-per-commit or update-never, contradicting Section 14's own risk row
findings.problem: The plan never states how `plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json`'s `version` will be set. If left unset on a git-hosted marketplace source, Claude Code derives the version from the git commit SHA, so the plugin auto-updates on every push; on an `npm` source, version always resolves to `unknown`, so `/plugin update` can never detect a new release at all. Either extreme undermines Section 14's own risk mitigation ('Pin tested Claude Code version in README').
findings.evidence: 'The git commit SHA of the plugin's source, for `github`, `url`, `git-subdir`, and relative-path sources in a git-hosted marketplace' (item 3) and '`unknown`, for `npm` sources' (item 5) -- cc_plugins_ref.md:1467-1471. VERDICT_PLAN.md:373 (Section 14 risk row): 'Hook schema changes in Claude Code | Pin tested Claude Code version in README; integration tests on captured stdin fixtures; nightly E2E catches breakage'.
findings.recommendation: Set an explicit `"version"` in `plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, bumped by CI on each git tag alongside the PyPI release (Section 10's tag-triggered publish step), so plugin marketplace users get controlled, deliberate updates rather than an update on every commit or no detectable update at all.

verifier.note: cc_plugins_ref.md:1467-1471 is verbatim: version resolves from plugin.json, then the marketplace entry, then (item 3) "The git commit SHA of the plugin's source, for `github`, `url`, `git-subdir`, and relative-path sources in a git-hosted marketplace", and (item 5) "`unknown`, for `npm` sources". :1463 confirms the version is the cache key that decides whether an update is available, and the approaches table at :1480-1481 states the consequence directly — explicit version means "Users get updates only when you bump this field", commit-SHA means "Users get updates whenever the source's resolved commit changes". VERDICT_PLAN.md:373 is quoted correctly. Recommendation is feasible and matches the doc's own "Best for: published plugins with stable release cycles" guidance plus its semver + CHANGELOG.md advice at :1484.
